questions.question: OpenStack was launched in 2010 as a joint project between Rackspace Hosting and which other organization?
questions.explanation: OpenStack, a software used to create cloud infrastructure, was launched as a joint project of Rackspace Hosting and NASA in 2010, and is open source.

questions.question: Which OpenStack component provides the dashboard (GUI) that gives an overview of the other components?
questions.explanation: Horizon is the dashboard component of OpenStack — it provides the GUI of the software and gives an overview of the other components.

questions.question: Which OpenStack component is the compute service where instances are launched?
questions.explanation: Nova is the compute service in OpenStack — it is where you launch your instances. Glance is the image service, Cinder is block storage, and Neutron provides networking.

questions.question: Which script/tool is used in the lecture to install OpenStack, requiring the local.conf file to be configured with passwords and host IP before running?
questions.explanation: OpenStack is installed using Devstack: after cloning the devstack repository and configuring local.conf with ADMIN_PASSWORD, DATABASE_PASSWORD, RABBIT_PASSWORD, SERVICE_PASSWORD, and HOST_IP, the stack.sh file is run to install it.

questions.question: According to the lecture, what does sensor-cloud fundamentally provide, beyond merely integrating sensors with cloud computing?
options: A physical replacement for all sensor hardware
Virtualization of sensor nodes, offered on a pay-per-use basis
A way to eliminate the need for a sink node
questions.explanation: Sensor-cloud is not mere integration of sensors and cloud computing or 'dumping sensor data into the cloud' — it introduces the concept of virtualization of the sensor node, offered on a pay-per-use basis, acting as a stratum between sensor nodes and end-users.
questions.source: See Lecture 42 (Sensor-Cloud – Part I: Sensor-as-a-Service, slide 10)

questions.question: In a traditional Wireless Sensor Network (WSN), who is typically responsible for redeployment of the sensor nodes?
questions.explanation: In a traditional WSN, the WSN-user is responsible for ownership, deployment, redeployment, maintenance, overhead, and usage. In sensor-cloud, redeployment and maintenance shift to the Sensor-Cloud Service Provider (SCSP), while usage shifts to the end-user.
questions.source: See Lecture 42 (Sensor-Cloud – Part I: Sensor-as-a-Service, slide 12)

questions.question: In the sensor-cloud model, which actor purchases physical sensor devices and lends them to the sensor- cloud, playing a role from a business perspective?
questions.explanation: The Sensor-owner purchases physical sensor devices deployed over different geographical locations and lends these devices to the sensor-cloud, acting as a business actor.
questions.source: See Lecture 42 (Sensor-Cloud – Part I: Sensor-as-a-Service, slide 13)

questions.question: Which of the following is listed as a major limitation of traditional WSNs that motivates the sensor- cloud model?
options: Difficulty adapting to a change of requirement (e.g., moving from agriculture to smart home use)
questions.explanation: Limitations of WSNs include procurement issues (price, right vendor, sensor types), deployment and maintenance overheads, and difficulty adapting to a change of requirement — e.g., a WSN built for agriculture cannot easily be repurposed for a smart home.
questions.source: See Lecture 42 (Sensor-Cloud – Part I: Sensor-as-a-Service, slide 9)

questions.question: In the Optimal Composition of Virtual Sensors, what does CoV-I refer to?
options: Composition of virtual sensors spanning multiple geographic regions
Composition of virtual sensors using only homogeneous nodes within the same geographic region
A caching mechanism for sensor data
questions.explanation: CoV-I refers to the formation of a Virtual Sensor (VS) using homogeneous sensor nodes within the same geographical boundary, while CoV-II spans multiple regions using heterogeneous nodes to form a Virtual Sensor Group (VSG).
questions.source: See Lecture 43 (Sensor-Cloud – Part II: Sensor-as-a-Service, slide 6)

questions.question: In the sensor-cloud caching mechanism, which cache handles requests directly from the end-user and decides whether to serve data directly or re-cache from another source?
questions.explanation: The Internal Cache (IC) handles requests from the end-user and takes the decision on whether the data should be provided directly or whether it is required to re-cache the data from the External Cache (EC).
questions.source: See Lecture 43 (Sensor-Cloud – Part II: Sensor-as-a-Service, slide 13)

questions.question: Why is dynamic and adaptive data caching useful in sensor-cloud, according to the lecture?
options: Because environmental conditions always change extremely fast
Because it removes the need for a sensor-owner
Because caching eliminates the need for virtualization
Because unnecessary sensing during slow environmental change wastes energy
questions.explanation: In many cases, environmental conditions change quite slowly, so the sensed data of physical sensors remains largely unaltered; unnecessary sensing under such conditions causes needless energy consumption, motivating adaptive caching.
questions.source: See Lecture 43 (Sensor-Cloud – Part II: Sensor-as-a-Service, slide 12)

questions.question: Which company is credited with coining the term 'fog computing'?
questions.explanation: Fog computing, or 'fogging,' is a term coined by CISCO. The idea is to extend the cloud nearer to IoT devices by introducing an intermediate layer between the cloud and the devices.
questions.source: See Lecture 44 (Fog Computing – Part I, slide 2)

questions.question: Which of the following is listed as a key issue with the traditional cloud model that motivates fog computing?
options: Volume, latency, and bandwidth limitations of the cloud
Too much local processing power at the device level
questions.explanation: The current cloud model faces issues of Volume (too much data to process/store), Latency (round-trip time is too slow for time-sensitive data), and Bandwidth (huge traffic generated by billions of devices consumes most available bandwidth).
questions.source: See Lecture 44 (Fog Computing – Part I, slide 6)

questions.question: Where is the fog layer positioned in the fog computing architecture?
options: Between the cloud and the IoT devices
There is no fixed position; it replaces the cloud entirely
questions.explanation: Fog is a layer between the cloud and IoT devices; many fog nodes can be present, and sensor data are processed in the fog before being sent to the cloud, reducing latency and saving bandwidth and cloud storage.
questions.source: See Lecture 45 (Fog Computing – Part II, slide 2)

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a required characteristic of a fog node?
questions.explanation: Fog nodes need transient storage, computing facility (to process data and take quick decisions), and network connectivity to connect with IoT devices, other fog nodes, and the cloud — not permanent unlimited archival storage, which is the cloud's role.
questions.source: See Lecture 45 (Fog Computing – Part II, slide 4)
